@graph.name: How to pitch Cointelegraph and earn editorial coverage
@graph.description: A 7-step practitioner's playbook for landing earned Cointelegraph coverage in 2026, from mapping the right newsroom surface to sending complete materials and following up once.

tool.name: A dated news peg (launch, listing, deadline, funding close, market move)
Writer beat map (Google site search of cointelegraph.com)
One-page fact sheet with named quotes, data, and high-resolution founder photos

step.name: Understand how Cointelegraph's newsroom is actually built
step.text: Treat Cointelegraph as several distinct surfaces, not one inbox. The news desk runs fast dated news and filters for a real peg; markets and analysis run price, on-chain data and trend pieces and filter for original data; opinion, features and the sponsored side each filter for something different. Map your story to the right surface before you write a word.

step.name: Lead with a dated news peg, not a product
step.text: Editors decide in roughly 15 seconds and look first for why this story matters now. Anchor the story to a date: a launch day, a listing, a regulatory deadline, a market move, or a funding close. Without a peg even good news reads as evergreen, and evergreen sinks to the bottom of the pile.

step.name: Find the right writer, then prove you read them
step.text: Cointelegraph has a large rotating staff and contributor pool across DeFi, infrastructure, regulation, markets, NFTs and gaming, AI, and regional desks. Do not pitch the editor. Pitch the one writer whose last few pieces sit next to your story, and reference a specific recent piece to prove you read it. A Google site search of cointelegraph.com is the fastest way to map beats.

step.name: Write the under-150-word pitch
step.text: Plain-text email, no attachments or decks in the first message. Four short paragraphs doing four jobs: the peg, why it matters to that writer's beat, the proof, and a clear path to finishing the piece. Put the dated peg in the subject line and the first sentence.

step.name: Respect the editorial and sponsored firewall
step.text: Cointelegraph runs a clearly labelled sponsored and brand-content business alongside its firewalled newsroom. Paying for sponsored placement does not move your odds with an editorial writer, and implying it should is the fastest way to get ignored. Pick the lane honestly: sponsored for guaranteed dated placement you control, editorial for credibility and AI-search citations you cannot buy.

step.name: Use the multilingual editions for real APAC reach
step.text: Most US-only PR plans miss this lever. Cointelegraph publishes regional editions in several languages, and the overnight liquidity windows for Web3 sit in Korea, Japan, Vietnam and Brazil. When the story has a regional angle, pitch the relevant edition with a localised peg and a domestic hook rather than a translated English release, and pair it with vetted regional KOLs.

step.name: Send complete materials, then follow up once
step.text: The biggest reason a yes turns into a no-show is incomplete materials. After the writer bites, send a tight package the writer can finish the piece from without chasing you: a one-page fact sheet, two named quotes, on-chain or product data, two high-resolution founder photos, and a one-paragraph bio. Then follow up once, not five times.

mainEntity.name: How do you pitch Cointelegraph and actually get a reply?

acceptedAnswer.text: Lead the subject line and first line with a dated news peg that answers why the story matters now. Pitch one named writer whose recent work matches your beat, not a press list, and reference a specific recent piece of theirs to prove you read it. Keep the email under 150 words, in plain text, and offer complete materials: a one-page fact sheet, data, a named spokesperson, and a clear path to finishing the story without ten follow-ups.

Cointelegraph runs a clearly labelled sponsored and brand-content business that is paid, but its newsroom coverage is earned and firewalled from that side. Paying for sponsored placement does not improve your odds with an editorial writer, and implying it should is a fast way to get ignored. Choose the lane honestly: sponsored for guaranteed dated placement you control, editorial for credibility and AI-search citations you cannot buy.

mainEntity.name: How is pitching Cointelegraph different from pitching CoinDesk?

acceptedAnswer.text: Both want a category-level story over an announcement, but the emphasis differs. Cointelegraph rewards a sharp dated news peg, original data or a price angle, and it has strong multilingual regional editions that open Korea, Japan, Vietnam and Brazil. CoinDesk leans toward the canonical narrative and tighter embargo coordination. Map your story to the right outlet and the right internal surface rather than blasting both with the same note.

mainEntity.name: Can I use the Cointelegraph regional editions for APAC reach?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, and most US-only plans miss this. Cointelegraph publishes editions in several languages, and the overnight liquidity windows for Web3 sit in Asia and Brazil. When your story has a regional angle, pitch the relevant edition with a localised peg and a domestic hook rather than a translated English release, and pair it with vetted regional KOLs to cover the windows the English desk sleeps through.

mainEntity.name: How long does it take to land Cointelegraph coverage?

acceptedAnswer.text: News-desk coverage tied to a dated peg typically moves in days to two weeks from first contact, if the peg is real and materials are complete. A Cointelegraph Magazine feature or founder profile takes longer, often three to six weeks, because it needs multiple conversations and an editor's sign-off. Opinion submissions sit in between and depend on the strength of the argument and the timeliness of the topic.
